_note: Biographical roster of the 36 voices whose Bani is in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (schema v2). Presentation data only: it never alters scripture. 'name' is the corpus author string; counts and Angs always come from the database. Life facts come only from the tier-2 sources in each entry's 'sources' (see 'source_index'); a null date is unknown, never guessed, and 'range_note' says why. Every entry is a draft until the G3 scholar review marks it approved. Historical context, never a ranking.

contributors.name: Guru Nanak Dev Ji (M1)
contributors.birthplace: Rai Bhoi ki Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib (Pakistan)

notable.title: Japji Sahib
Asa di Vaar
Dakhni Oankar
Sidh Gosht
Barah Maha (Tukhari)

contributors.blurb: The first Guru and founder of the Sikh faith; the Granth opens with his Mool Mantar and Japji.
contributors.context: Guru Nanak was born on 15 April 1469 at Rai Bhoi ki Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib. After years of travel he settled around 1521 at Kartarpur, where he joined devotion to God with the life of a householder. Before his death on 7 September 1539 he installed Bhai Lahina, whom he renamed Angad, as his successor.

sources.entry: Japji, Ang 1; Asa di Vaar, Ang 462; Oankar, Ang 929; Sidh Gosht, Ang 938; Barah Maha, Ang 1107

contributors.name: Guru Angad Dev Ji (M2)
contributors.birthplace: Matte di Sarai, now Sarai Naga, near Muktsar (Punjab)
contributors.blurb: The second Guru; his Bani is saloks, set within the Vaars of the Granth.
contributors.context: Guru Angad was born Lahina on 31 March 1504 at Matte di Sarai, now Sarai Naga. Guru Nanak named him his successor. He passed away at Khadur on 29 March 1552, handing the succession to Guru Amar Das.

contributors.name: Guru Amar Das Ji (M3)

notable.title: Anand Sahib

contributors.blurb: The third Guru; author of the Anand Sahib.
contributors.context: Guru Amar Das was born on 5 May 1479 at Basarke and became Guru in 1552, after Guru Angad. Goindval, a settlement he founded at Guru Angad's bidding, was his seat. Before his death on 1 September 1574 he chose Bhai Jetha, his son-in-law, as his successor, Guru Ram Das.

contributors.name: Guru Ram Das Ji (M4)

notable.title: Laavan

contributors.blurb: The fourth Guru, who founded Amritsar; his Laavan are sung at the Sikh wedding.
contributors.context: Guru Ram Das was born Jetha on 24 September 1534 in Chuna Mandi, Lahore, and lived at Goindval near Guru Amar Das, who chose him as successor. He founded the settlement that became Amritsar, and he died at Goindval on 1 September 1581.

contributors.name: Guru Arjan Dev Ji (M5)

notable.title: Sukhmani Sahib
Bavan Akhri
Barah Maha (Majh)
Mundavani

contributors.blurb: The fifth Guru, who compiled the Adi Granth (installed 1604); the author of Sukhmani Sahib.
contributors.context: Guru Arjan was born on 15 April 1563 at Goindval, the son of Guru Ram Das and Bibi Bhani. He compiled the Adi Granth, installed in the Harimandar on 16 August 1604; over a third of it is his own Bani. He was the first martyr of the Sikh faith, at Lahore on 30 May 1606.

sources.entry: Sukhmani, Ang 262; Bavan Akhri, Ang 250; Barah Maha, Ang 133; Mundavani, Ang 1429

contributors.name: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji (M9)

notable.title: Salok Mahala 9

contributors.blurb: The ninth Guru, martyred at Delhi in 1675; his saloks close the Bani of the Gurus in the Granth.
contributors.context: Guru Tegh Bahadur, youngest son of Guru Hargobind, was born at Amritsar on 1 April 1621. He founded Chakk Nanaki, later Anandpur, naming it after his mother. He was beheaded in public in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, on 11 November 1675, having named his son Gobind Das as his successor.

contributors.name: Sheikh Farid Ji

notable.title: Saloks of Sheikh Farid

contributors.blurb: Sufi mystic, known as the first recorded poet of the Punjabi language.
contributors.context: Shaikh Farid was born in AD 1173 (569 AH) at Kothewal, near Multan, and died in 1265. A Sufi of the Chishti order, he set up a centre at Hansi and later at Ajodhan, now Pakpattan. He is known as the first recorded poet of the Punjabi language.

contributors.name: Bhagat Jaidev Ji
contributors.range_note: No birth or death year is recorded. He flourished under Rajas of Orissa of AD 1142–56 and 1170–80, and Raja Lakshman Sen of Bengal (AD 1175–1200) became his disciple.
contributors.birthplace: Kindu Bilva: Kenduli (Birbhum, West Bengal) or Kenduli-Sasan (near Puri, Odisha), as sources differ

notable.title: Maru shabad
notable.gurmukhi: ਰਾਗੁ ਮਾਰੂ ਬਾਣੀ ਜੈਦੇਉ ਜੀਉ ਕੀ
notable.anchor: ਚੰਦ ਸਤ ਭੇਦਿਆ ਨਾਦ ਸਤ ਪੂਰਿਆ ਸੂਰ ਸਤ ਖੋੜਸਾ ਦਤੁ ਕੀਆ

contributors.blurb: Poet of the Gita Govinda; two of his hymns are in the Granth.
contributors.context: Jaidev is chiefly known as the author of the Gita Govinda. He was born at Kindu Bilva, identified with Kenduli in Bengal or Kenduli-Sasan near Puri, and died in his birth village. Two of his hymns are in the Granth.
contributors.disputed: His birthplace is disputed: Kenduli in Bengal or Kenduli-Sasan near Puri in Odisha.

contributors.name: Bhagat Trilochan Ji
contributors.range_note: Born 1267, as the EoS reports; no death year is recorded.
contributors.blurb: A Maharashtrian sant, learned in Puranic lore; four of his hymns are in the Granth.
contributors.context: Trilochan was a Maharashtrian saint-poet, said to have been born in 1267 to a Vaishya family. Four of his hymns are in the Granth, in Siri, Gujri and Dhanasri. Two saloks among Kabir's present a dialogue between him and Namdev.

sources.entry: Siri, Ang 92; Gujri, Ang 525; Dhanasri, Ang 695

notes: Inside the Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (Angs 1364–1377), saloks 212–213 (Ang 1375–1376) are a dialogue signed by Namdev and Trilochan, salok 241 is signed by Namdev and salok 242 by Ravidas (Ang 1377). Today's corpus credits them to Guru Arjan (a header bleed); sggs-data 1.1.0 credits them to Bhagat Kabir Ji as part of his collection and flags them for review. Scholar to rule whether each is shown under Kabir or under the voice that signs it.

contributors.disputed: Scholars disagree on his birthplace: Barsi (Sholapur district) or Uttar Pradesh.

contributors.name: Bhagat Namdev Ji
contributors.range_note: 1270–1350 is the generally accepted traditional date.
contributors.blurb: Marathi sant of fervent devotion; sixty-one of his hymns are in the Granth.
contributors.context: Namdev was born in 1270 at Narasi-Vamani in Maharashtra, to a tailor's family, and turned to bhakti under Jnanadeva. He is said to have lived for over twenty years at Ghuman in the Punjab, and later settled at Pandharpur. Sixty-one of his hymns are in the Granth.

notes: Inside the Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (Angs 1364–1377), saloks 212–213 (Ang 1375–1376) are a dialogue signed by Namdev and Trilochan, salok 241 is signed by Namdev and salok 242 by Ravidas (Ang 1377). Today's corpus credits them to Guru Arjan (a header bleed); sggs-data 1.1.0 credits them to Bhagat Kabir Ji as part of his collection and flags them for review. Scholar to rule whether each is shown under Kabir or under the voice that signs it.

contributors.name: Bhagat Ramanand Ji
contributors.range_note: EoS headwords give 1300–1410; its other entries give 1299–1410 and 1300–1411.
contributors.blurb: Teacher of Vaishnava bhakti at Kashi; his single hymn in the Granth rejects idol-worship.
contributors.context: Ramanand was born at Prayag and taught at Kashi, where he founded the Ramanandi sampradaya. Tradition names Kabir, Ravidas, Sain and Dhanna among his disciples, though the dates make this impossible for all of them. His one hymn in the Granth (Basant, Ang 1195) rejects idol-worship.

contributors.name: Bhagat Kabir Ji
contributors.range_note: Born 1398. He died in 1518 by the traditional (Kabirpanthi) account, or in 1448 by recent scholarship (Dvivedi, Vaudeville).

notable.title: Bavan Akhri
Thiti
Var Sat (the seven days)
Saloks of Bhagat Kabir

contributors.blurb: The weaver-mystic of Kashi; his Bani is the largest of any Bhagat in the Granth.
contributors.context: Kabir's life centred on Kashi (Banaras), where he worked as a weaver. Of all the Bhagats his contribution to the Granth is the largest: 227 padas in 17 raags and 237 saloks. He spent his last days at Magahar rather than Banaras.

sources.entry: Siri, Ang 92; Gauri, Angs 340–344; Saloks, Ang 1364

notes: Inside the Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (Angs 1364–1377), saloks 212–213 (Ang 1375–1376) are a dialogue signed by Namdev and Trilochan, salok 241 is signed by Namdev and salok 242 by Ravidas (Ang 1377). Today's corpus credits them to Guru Arjan (a header bleed); sggs-data 1.1.0 credits them to Bhagat Kabir Ji as part of his collection and flags them for review. Scholar to rule whether each is shown under Kabir or under the voice that signs it.

contributors.name: Bhagat Ravidas Ji
contributors.range_note: No birth or death year is recorded; the EoS places him in the 15th century (fl.).
contributors.blurb: Poet and mystic of Varanasi who rejected caste; forty of his hymns are in the Granth.
contributors.context: Ravidas was born near Varanasi to a family of leather-workers and followed the family trade. He came to reject idol-worship and distinctions of caste, and Mirabai was among his followers. Forty of his hymns are in the Granth.

notes: Inside the Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (Angs 1364–1377), saloks 212–213 (Ang 1375–1376) are a dialogue signed by Namdev and Trilochan, salok 241 is signed by Namdev and salok 242 by Ravidas (Ang 1377). Today's corpus credits them to Guru Arjan (a header bleed); sggs-data 1.1.0 credits them to Bhagat Kabir Ji as part of his collection and flags them for review. Scholar to rule whether each is shown under Kabir or under the voice that signs it.

contributors.name: Bhagat Beni Ji
contributors.range_note: Very little is known of his life, and no dates are recorded.
contributors.blurb: A sant of single-minded meditation; three of his hymns are in the Granth.
contributors.context: Very little is known of Beni's life except his devotion to prayer and meditation; Bhai Gurdas refers to it. Three of his hymns are in the Granth, in Siri, Ramkali and Prabhati. Guru Arjan directed that the Siri hymn be sung in the tune of Guru Nanak's Pahire.

contributors.name: Bhagat Bhikhan Ji
contributors.range_note: 1480–1573, as the EoS headword gives.
contributors.blurb: A sant in the tradition of Ravidas and Dhanna; two of his hymns are in the Granth.
contributors.context: Bhakta Bhikhan was a devotee in the tradition of Ravidas and Dhanna; he is distinct from a Sufi of the same name and time. His two hymns in the Granth call the Name of Hari the cure for all the ills of the world.

contributors.name: Bhagat Dhanna Ji
contributors.range_note: Born 1415 by Macauliffe's reckoning, which the EoS reports; no death year is recorded. The earliest mention of him is by Mirabai (1498–1546).
contributors.blurb: A Jatt farmer of Rajasthan, drawn to devotion by Namdev, Kabir, Ravidas and Sain; three hymns are his.
contributors.context: Dhanna was born in the village of Dhuan in Tonk district, Rajasthan, the son of a farmer. In a hymn in Asa he tells how the examples of Namdev, Kabir, Ravidas and Sain drew him to God. He turned from worshipping idols to the Formless One, and three of his hymns are in the Granth.

notes: Birthplace: the EoS names Dhuan (Tonk district). Discovery sources also name Dhuan Kalan and Chauru; no tier-2 source for either was found. Scholar to rule before any variant is shown.

contributors.name: Bhagat Sain Ji
contributors.range_note: No dates are recorded. Tradition makes him a disciple of Ramanand (1300–1411), drawn to him by Kabir's fame.
contributors.blurb: A barber-saint whose one hymn in the Granth calls praise of the Lord the true aarti.
contributors.context: All accounts agree that Sain was a barber. Bhai Gurdas makes him a disciple of Ramanand. Guru Arjan names him as a bhakta of rare devotion (Ang 487), and Ravidas ranks him with Namdev, Kabir, Trilochan and Sadhna (Ang 1106). His one hymn (Dhanasri, Ang 695) teaches that singing the Lord's praise and meditating on His Name are the highest worship.
contributors.disputed: Where he served is disputed: one tradition places him at the court of Rewa (Bandhavgarh) in Central India, another at Bidar in the South. No birthplace is given.

contributors.name: Bhagat Pipa Ji
contributors.range_note: Born about AD 1425; no death year is recorded.
contributors.blurb: A prince of Gagraun who gave up his throne; his one hymn finds the Divine within the body.
contributors.context: Pipa was a prince, born at Gagraun about 1425, who renounced his throne after initiation by Ramanand at Kashi. He later lived at Dwarka and gave up idol-worship. His one hymn in the Granth (Dhanasri, Ang 695) finds the Divine within the body.

contributors.name: Bhagat Sadhna Ji
contributors.range_note: No dates are recorded; he is considered a contemporary of Namdev (1270–1350).
contributors.blurb: A butcher by trade whose single hymn asks the Lord to save his honour.
contributors.context: Sadhna lived by selling meat and won spiritual eminence through devotion. He is believed to have been born at Sehwan in Sindh and was cremated at Sirhind, where a tomb honours him. His only hymn, in Bilaval (Ang 858), asks the Lord to save the honour of His servant.

contributors.name: Bhagat Parmanand Ji
contributors.range_note: Born probably in 1483; no death year is recorded.
contributors.blurb: A Maharashtrian saint-poet whose one hymn puts devotion and service above ritual reading.
contributors.context: Parmanand was a Maharashtrian saint-poet, born probably in 1483, who is believed to have lived at Barsi, north of Pandharpur. He wrote under the pen-name Sarang. His one hymn in the Granth (Sarang, Ang 1253) faults reading the scriptures as ritual when it does not lead to serving others.

sources.entry: Ang 1253: Sahib Singh's note on the Sarang Bhagat Bani tally (Parmanand 1 shabad)

contributors.name: Bhagat Surdas Ji
contributors.range_note: Said to have been born in 1529; he died at Banaras, and no year is recorded.
contributors.blurb: A bhakta poet of whom the Granth keeps one line, answered by a shabad of Guru Arjan.
contributors.context: Surdas, born Madan Mohan, is said to have been born in 1529 into a Brahmin family. He served Akbar as governor of Sandila, renounced the world, and died at Banaras. The Granth keeps one line of his, "ਛਾਡਿ ਮਨ ਹਰਿ ਬਿਮੁਖਨ ਕੋ ਸੰਗੁ" (Sarang, Ang 1253). The shabad after it, headed "ਸਾਰੰਗ ਮਹਲਾ ੫ ਸੂਰਦਾਸ", is Guru Arjan's, written in response.

sources.entry: Ang 1253: Sahib Singh's note: the single line is Surdas's; the next shabad is Mahala 5
Sarang, Ang 1253: line 53935 and the header ਸਾਰੰਗ ਮਹਲਾ ੫ ਸੂਰਦਾਸ

contributors.disputed: Only one line is his, and it carries no pen-name. The EoS and Sahib Singh agree that the following shabad is Guru Arjan's, though it names Surdas where the Gurus usually sign ਨਾਨਕ. This Surdas is distinct from the blind poet of the Sur Sagar; Sahib Singh notes that some scholars hold there were two Surdases.
contributors.attribution_note: The corpus files his single line (Ang 1253, ਛਾਡਿ ਮਨ ਹਰਿ ਬਿਮੁਖਨ ਕੋ ਸੰਗੁ) under Namdev; no heading or signature is printed with it, so the attribution is with a scholar for review.

contributors.name: Bhai Mardana
contributors.birthplace: Talwandi Rai Bhoe, now Nankana Sahib (Pakistan)
contributors.blurb: Guru Nanak's companion and rabab player on his travels. Saloks at Ang 553 carry his name (ਮਰਦਾਨਾ ੧); many read them as Guru Nanak's words addressed to him — under scholarly review.
contributors.context: Mardana was born in 1459 at Talwandi Rai Bhoe to a Mirasi family of hereditary minstrels. He grew up with Guru Nanak, was ten years his senior, and played the rabab as the Guru sang on all his travels. He died at Kartarpur in 1534.

sources.entry: Ang 553: Sahib Singh's note on the three saloks headed ਮਰਦਾਨਾ ੧
Bihagare ki Vaar, Ang 553 (header ਸਲੋਕੁ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ ੧)

contributors.disputed: Scholars dispute the attribution. The EoS holds that one salok at Ang 553 is Mardana's and two are Guru Nanak's addressed to him. Sahib Singh (Darpan, Ang 553) holds that all three are Guru Nanak's, because the lines sign ਨਾਨਕਾ/ਨਾਨਕ, which Mardana could not use. Kept in the roster and flagged for the scholar.

contributors.name: Baba Sundar Ji
contributors.range_note: No dates are recorded. He was the great-grandson of Guru Amar Das (1479–1574).

notable.title: Ramkali Sadu

contributors.blurb: Author of the Sadu, which tells of Guru Amar Das's peaceful, God-willed passing.
contributors.context: Sundar was the great-grandson of Guru Amar Das: his father was Anand Das, son of Baba Mohri. His six-stanza Ramkali Sadu tells of Guru Amar Das's last counsel, not to mourn him, and of his appointing Ram Das as successor. The Sadu is commonly read when a reading of the Granth concludes as part of the obsequies.

contributors.name: Satta & Balwand
contributors.display: Bhai Satta Ji & Bhai Balwand Ji
contributors.gurmukhi: ਭਾਈ ਸੱਤਾ ਜੀ ਤੇ ਭਾਈ ਬਲਵੰਡ ਜੀ
contributors.range_note: No dates are recorded. Both were contemporaries of Guru Arjan (1563–1606) and died at Lahore in Guru Hargobind's time.

notable.title: Ramkali ki Vaar (Tikke di Vaar)

contributors.blurb: The two rababis whose Vaar praises the one light passing from Guru to Guru.
contributors.context: Rai Balwand and Satta, said to be brothers, were Muslim Mirasi minstrels who played the rabab for Guru Arjan. Their Ramkali ki Vaar, known as Tikke di Vaar, sees all the Gurus as sharing one light. Both died at Lahore in the time of Guru Hargobind and were buried on the bank of the Ravi.

contributors.name: Bhatt Kalsahar (ਭਟ)
contributors.range_note: No birth or death year is recorded. The Bhatts were bards of the Gurus' court from Guru Amar Das's time to Guru Arjan's, and Guru Arjan included their Swaiyye in the Granth.

contributors.blurb: The Bhatts were bards of Brahmin families from the banks of the Sarasvati; some had settled at Sultanpur Lodhi.
contributors.context: The Bhatts were bards of Brahmin families from the banks of the Sarasvati; some had settled at Sultanpur Lodhi. Their Swaiyye (Angs 1389–1409) praise the Gurus not as individuals but as one light passing from body to body. This entry holds the Swaiyye headers and the lines the corpus does not credit to a named Bhatt.
